correctness.rationale: A uniform labeled double-occurrence word maps to a uniform perfect matching (each matching has exactly q! labelings). A length-2k Abelian-square window entails a perfect cross-half pairing, yielding exact probability k!(2q-2k-1)!!/(2q-1)!!. The expected-count sequence has strictly increasing successive ratio and exponentially small end term; the full longer-window sum is 2/(2q-1)+O(q^-2). For adjacent matched pairs, counting disjoint edges of a length-2q path yields the exact binomial moments; their comparison with Poisson(1) moments via binomial inversion and absolute summation proves O(1/q) in total variation. Exhaustive q=1..7 checks of every window/moment matched. No finite experiment is used to prove the infinite limit.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Fixed-alphabet average factor counts cannot give Poisson(1) in a family whose alphabet increases with length and every symbol has multiplicity exactly two. Arbitrary shuffle-square existence does not force any contiguous equal-Parikh adjacent halves. Standard Poisson laws for sparse matching edges cover only half-length one, leaving the substantial task of uniformly excluding longer windows.

originality.rationale: The specific result is a quantitative Poisson(1) limit for the total number of contiguous Abelian-square occurrences in uniformly random double-occurrence words, including a 1/q total-variation rate, exact finite-window expectations, and negligible longer windows. The inspected full-text material concerns fixed-alphabet Abelian repetitions, structural insertions in double-occurrence words, or noncontiguous shuffle squares; their conclusions do not imply these statements. Poisson limits for selected rare matching edges are recognized as related foundational methodology, not claimed as original. Relevant exact terms and mathematical implications were searched in available literature and mathematical-record indexes. No exact prior theorem was identified; unindexed equivalence remains a risk.

value.rationale: Abelian-square avoidance is a central phenomenon in word combinatorics; doubling each symbol while letting the alphabet grow is a natural non-iid occupancy model from double-occurrence/Gauss words. The result shows a quantitatively sharp phase distinction: unlike a fixed-binary-alphabet random word with many repetitions, a uniform double-occurrence word has only Poisson(1) total local Abelian-square occurrences and a nonzero limiting global avoidance probability. The exact cross-matching window probability plus O(1/q) all-length suppression identifies the structural reason and is useful in studying rare contiguous patterns in chord diagrams.
